docs.title: Bundled demo
docs.text: The bundled demo is a subset of OneStop Eye Movements. If you use it, also cite Berzak et al. (2025), OneStop: A 360-Participant English Eye Tracking Dataset with Different Reading Regimes, Scientific Data. DOI: 10.1038/s41597-025-06272-2.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: With the desktop app or a local install, your recordings stay on your computer and are processed locally. The online demo processes the files you upload on its hosted server. Help → About says which of the two you are using.

docs.title: Your data
docs.text:
A local install (scanpath-studio) and the desktop app save your work on your computer, so a refresh or a restart picks up where you left off.

  • What is saved: the datasets you added, with their column mappings, your annotations, your saved designs, attached metadata tables, and your view, trial and plot settings. The bundled demo and public datasets are not copied, since they reload from their source.
  • Where: ~/.cache/scanpath-studio/session-v1 in your home folder (C:\Users\<you>\.cache\scanpath-studio\session-v1 on Windows), or the folder SCANPATH_STUDIO_STATE_DIR names. Data Management → Saved on this computer shows the folder and what it holds, and so does scanpath-studio cache.
  • How long: until you clear it. Removing a dataset from the app removes its saved copy.
  • To clear it: Clear what is saved… under Saved on this computer, or close the app and run scanpath-studio cache --clear.
  • To turn it off: start the app with scanpath-studio --no-persist, or set SCANPATH_STUDIO_PERSIST=0.
  • Downloaded public datasets stay in the folders you downloaded them to, and clearing what is saved leaves them. Saved on this computer lists them beside the datasets you added, each with its size and folder. Its button deletes that download's files, after a confirmation, and leaves anything else in the folder.

The online demo saves nothing. A file you upload there is processed on Streamlit Community Cloud and not kept, so closing or refreshing the tab loses it. The app itself has no analytics, but Community Cloud's page around the app does; see its privacy policy. Export your annotations and settings before you leave (what to back up).

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The public API follows one pipeline:

load data → list trials → plot → save

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_scanpath_data("ia.csv", "fixations.csv")
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, participant="p1", trial="t3")
sps.save_figure(fig, "scanpath.html")

Every function on this page is importable from scanpath_studio. The figure builders also take the figure options as keywords.

docs.title: Column names
docs.text:
Columns keep the names your files give them. The bundled demo's Words table calls its word ID column IA_ID and its total fixation duration IA_DWELL_TIME, and every function and option takes those names. A column Scanpath Studio made keeps its internal name. load_scanpath_data(..., names="canonical") gives the internal names, which are the same for every dataset. On the bundled demo, the first steps print this (run when the docs are built):

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
print(sps.list_trials(words, fixations).head(3))

columns = ["IA_ID", "IA_LABEL", "IA_FIRST_FIXATION_DURATION", "IA_DWELL_TIME"]
print(words[columns].head(3))

docs.title: load_scanpath_data
docs.text:
load_scanpath_data(
    words=None,
    fixations=None,
    *,
    word_schema=None,
    fix_schema=None,
    trial_parts_manifest=None,
    image_root=None,
    image_pattern=DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN,
    keep_columns=None,
    names=NAMES_SOURCE,
)

Load and normalize a Words table, a Fixations table, or both.

Columns keep the names your files give them: CURRENT_FIX_DURATION, not duration_ms. A column Scanpath Studio built, converted, computed or changed keeps its internal name, and data.column_names records what every column was called. Every API function takes these frames, and every column option (color_by=, the hover fields …) takes either name.

Columns are auto-detected from EyeLink, Gazepoint, Tobii, SMI, Pupil Labs and snake_case names. Normalization keeps the mapped fields and the recognized optional ones (eye, EyeLink's interest-area measures, linguistic features …) and drops the rest, unless keep_columns names them.

  • One table is enough. Leave out the table a dataset doesn't have: it comes back as an empty frame, and the plots skip that layer.
  • Stimulus-level words. A Words table without a participant column holds each text's word boxes once, and they are copied onto every trial in the fixations. Each trial is matched by its trial ID, else the trial ID it had before a repeat's _r2 suffix, else its text_id (for trial IDs that embed the participant). Trials that match none raise a data.StimulusJoinWarning (a UserWarning).
  • Fixations without x/y but with a word ID are placed at the centers of their word boxes.
  • Text word IDs. A word ID column that holds text and no numbers (w1, Hello_3) is read as keys, kept in a word_key column (under the column's own name with names="source"). Each word's word_id is then its position in its text, 1, 2, … in the Words table's row order (the order of the reading that lists the most of the text), one number for every reader, and a fixation's is the number of the word with the same text ID in its trial — exactly the same text, else none. A text ID never matches a number.
  • Bookkeeping columns. Columns named in data.INTERNAL_COLUMNS are the pipeline's own; data.drop_internal_columns removes them.

Parameters:

  • words (TablesLike | None, default: None ) –

    The Words table, one word box per row: a DataFrame; a .csv, .tsv, .txt, .tab, .parquet, .feather, .xlsx or .xls file, or a .zip of them; a glob pattern; or a list of paths. Several files (one per participant and/or text) are concatenated, with each file's stem in a source_file column.

  • fixations (TablesLike | None, default: None ) –

    The Fixations table, in any form words takes.

  • word_schema (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A mapping from field to column name for the Words table, replacing auto-detection. Start from propose_schema.

  • fix_schema (dict | None, default: None ) –

    The same for the Fixations table.

  • trial_parts_manifest (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A nested parent-trial/parts definition, for datasets whose tables identify screens through arbitrary selector columns. Explicit screen_id / screen_index columns can instead be mapped in each schema.

  • image_root (str | Path | None, default: None ) –

    A local folder of stimulus images, one page per trial (or screen). Each row the pattern finds a file for gets it as its image_path; a row without one keeps the image_path it had. show_stimulus_image=True then draws the page under the figure. attach_stimulus_images does the same for frames already loaded.

  • image_pattern (str, default: DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN ) –

    The file to look for under image_root, with {placeholders} naming the rows' canonical columns: "{text_id}.png", "{participant_id}/{trial_id}.png".

  • keep_columns (Iterable[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Further columns of your own to carry through under their own names, such as a pupil size or a detection confidence, from whichever table has them, so a figure can color, hover or plot by them. The app's Extra fields to keep; render --keep-columns.

  • names (str, default: NAMES_SOURCE ) –

    "source" keeps the dataset's column names; "canonical" returns the internal names, the same for every dataset, for code that works across datasets.

Returns:

  • ScanpathData –

    The normalized (words, fixations) frames, as a ScanpathData.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    A required field can't be found. The message names the field, the column names auto-detection looked for, and the columns the table has.

  • ValueError –

    image_root does not exist, or image_pattern is absolute or climbs out of it.

  • StimulusJoinError –

    A stimulus-level Words table shares neither a trial ID nor a text_id with any trial (or, multipart, with every screen a trial has fixations on). A ValueError.

  • UnplacedFixationsError –

    The fixations have no x/y, and not one of their word IDs names a word: text IDs the Words table does not have, or numbers against a Words table of text IDs. A ValueError.

docs.title: ScanpathData
docs.text:
Bases: tuple

The (words, fixations) frames load_scanpath_data returns, with their names.

It is a tuple, so words, fixations = load_scanpath_data(…) unpacks it, and .words / .fixations name the two frames. column_names holds the dataset's own name for every canonical column, per table: {"words": ColumnNames, "fixations": ColumnNames}.

With names="source" (the default) the frames' columns are the dataset's own names and each frame carries its map, so any API function takes it, sliced, filtered or merged, and the names it writes are yours. With names="canonical" they are the internal names, the same for every dataset.

docs.title: propose_schema
docs.text:
propose_schema(table, kind='words')

Find the column mapping auto-detection would use for a raw table.

It is the mapping load_scanpath_data infers, so it is the place to start when detection got a field wrong or could not find one: edit the dict and pass it back as word_schema= or fix_schema=.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A raw, not yet normalized table: a DataFrame, a path, a glob or a list of paths, as the loader takes.

  • kind (str, default: 'words' ) –

    "words", "fixations" or "raw_gaze".

Returns:

  • dict –

    {canonical field: source column}, with None for a field it could not find.

Examples:

schema = sps.propose_schema("ia.csv", "words")
schema["trial"] = "TRIAL_LABEL"
words, fixations = sps.load_scanpath_data(
    "ia.csv", "fix.csv", word_schema=schema
)

docs.title: attach_stimulus_images
docs.text:
attach_stimulus_images(
    words,
    fixations,
    image_root,
    image_pattern=DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN,
)

Fill image_path from a folder of stimulus images, on frames already loaded.

It is load_scanpath_data's image_root / image_pattern, for frames that came from somewhere else, such as a corpus loader, which takes no folder. The rules are the same: the placeholders name the rows' canonical columns, and a row the pattern finds no file for keeps the image_path it had.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None) –

    The words frame, or None.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None) –

    The fixations frame, or None.

  • image_root (str | Path) –

    The folder of stimulus images.

  • image_pattern (str, default: DEFAULT_STIMULUS_IMAGE_PATTERN ) –

    The file to look for under image_root, as in load_scanpath_data.

Returns:

  • ScanpathData –

    New (words, fixations) frames, under the names they came in. The frames passed in are not modified.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    image_root does not exist, or image_pattern is absolute or climbs out of it.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.attach_stimulus_images(
    *sps.load_potec("data/PoTeC", readers=[0], texts=["b0"]),
    "pages/",
    "{text_id}.png",
)
sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, show_stimulus_image=True)

docs.title: load_raw_gaze
docs.text:
load_raw_gaze(table, *, raw_gaze_schema=None, names=NAMES_SOURCE)

Load and normalize a raw, sample-level gaze table, for raw_gaze=.

Raw gaze is the third table plot_scanpath can draw, under the fixations: one row per eye-tracker sample, with a participant, a trial, x / y and usually a timestamp. plot_scanpath keeps only the plotted trial's (and screen's) samples, so one table can serve a whole corpus.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame, path, glob or list of paths, as load_scanpath_data takes. Columns are auto-detected the same way.

  • raw_gaze_schema (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A mapping from field to column, replacing auto-detection. Start from propose_schema(table, "raw_gaze").

  • names (str, default: NAMES_SOURCE ) –

    "source" keeps the table's column names; "canonical" returns the internal ones.

Returns:

  • DataFrame –

    The normalized samples.

Examples:

raw_gaze = sps.load_raw_gaze("gaze_samples.csv")
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, "p1", "t3", raw_gaze=raw_gaze)

docs.title: load_participant_metadata
docs.text:
load_participant_metadata(table, *, id_column=None, participants=None)

Load a participant-level metadata table: one row per participant.

Nothing is broadcast onto the words or fixations frames. Use scanpath_studio.metadata.project to attach chosen columns to a per-trial frame, or .values_for(pid) for one participant.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame, or a path or glob to a CSV, TSV, Parquet or Excel file, or a list of them, stacked into one table. It holds an ID column plus anything known about each participant (native_language, age, a comprehension score).

  • id_column (str | None, default: None ) –

    The participant ID column. Defaults to the first recognized spelling (participant_id, subject, RECORDING_SESSION_LABEL, …).

  • participants (DataFrame | list | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized frame or a list of IDs to validate the join against. The result's .report then names the participants missing from either side.

Returns:

  • ParticipantMetadata –

    A ParticipantMetadata: the cleaned frame, a field registry (name, label, grain, dtype, missingness) and the join report.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
meta = sps.load_participant_metadata("participants.csv", participants=fixations)
meta.names  # ('native_language', 'age')

docs.title: load_trial_metadata
docs.text:
load_trial_metadata(
    table, *, id_column=None, participant_column=None, trials=None
)

Load a trial-level metadata table: one row per trial.

The sibling of load_participant_metadata, one grain down. Nothing is broadcast onto the words or fixations frames.

The key is yours to state, and it changes what the table means. Keyed by trial ID alone, a row describes a text, and every trial of it inherits that row. Keyed by participant and trial (participant_column), a row describes one trial. Nothing in a file says which a corpus is, so this is never inferred.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame or file(s), as load_participant_metadata takes, stacked into one table. It holds a trial ID column plus anything known about each trial (a list name, a condition, a per-trial comprehension score).

  • id_column (str | None, default: None ) –

    The trial ID column. Defaults to the first recognized spelling (trial_id, item_id, TRIAL_INDEX, …).

  • participant_column (str | None, default: None ) –

    The participant ID column, to key each row by participant and trial. Left out, rows are keyed by trial ID alone.

  • trials (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized fixations or words frame, or any frame with participant_id and trial_id, to validate the join against. The result's .report then names the trials missing from either side.

Returns:

  • TrialMetadata –

    A TrialMetadata: the cleaned frame, a field registry and the join report.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
meta = sps.load_trial_metadata("readings.csv", trials=fixations)
meta.names  # ('list_name', 'comprehension_score')

docs.title: load_text_metadata
docs.text:
load_text_metadata(table, *, id_column=None, texts=None)

Load a text-level metadata table: one row per text.

A text is a stimulus, not something one participant owns, so the table is never keyed by participant. Nothing is broadcast onto the words or fixations frames.

Parameters:

  • table (TablesLike) –

    A DataFrame or file(s), as load_participant_metadata takes, stacked into one table. It holds a text ID column plus anything known about each text (genre, difficulty, a stimulus-level comprehension score).

  • id_column (str | list[str] | None, default: None ) –

    The text ID column, or several columns that build a composite ID, as the Text ID mapping can. Defaults to the first recognized spelling (text_id, paragraph_id, stimulus_id, …).

  • texts (DataFrame | list | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized fixations or words frame, or any iterable of text IDs, to validate the join against. The result's .report then names the texts missing from either side.

Returns:

  • TextMetadata –

    A TextMetadata: the cleaned frame, a field registry and the join report.

Examples:

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()
meta = sps.load_text_metadata("texts.csv", texts=words)
meta.names  # ('genre', 'difficulty')

Load the bundled demo, normalized and ready to plot.

The bundled demo is a subset of OneStop: two participants, twelve trials each, every one with fixations. The frames carry the demo's recorded screen (OneStop's 2560×1440), so plot_scanpath draws them on it without a canvas_size, as scanpath-studio render --sample does.

    "source" for the demo's own column names, "canonical" for the internal ones (see load_scanpath_data).

Returns:

    The (words, fixations) frames, as a ScanpathData.

docs.title: load_potec
docs.text:
load_potec(
    root, *, readers=None, texts=None, download=False, names="source"
)

Load PoTeC as normalized (words, fixations) frames, ready to plot.

A participant is a PoTeC reader id, as a string. A trial is one reader's reading of one text, <reader>_<text> ("0_b0"), and its text_id is the text: b0–b5 are biology, p0–p5 physics. The full corpus is 75 participants × 12 texts = 900 trials.

PoTeC's monitor was 1680×1050 (DELL P2210, 60 Hz). Pass that as canvas_size to plot_scanpath for true-to-scale rendering.

Parameters:

  • root (str | Path) –

    A clone of the PoTeC repository with its eye-tracking data downloaded, or any folder to download into.

  • readers (Iterable | None, default: None ) –

    Load only these readers ([0, 1]).

  • texts (Iterable[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Load only these texts (["b0", "p3"]).

  • download (bool, default: False ) –

    Fetch the files the load needs into root on first use, about 10 MB.

  • names (str, default: 'source' ) –

    "source" for PoTeC's own column names, "canonical" for the internal ones (see api.load_scanpath_data).

Returns:

  • tuple[DataFrame, DataFrame] –

    The normalized (words, fixations) frames.

Examples:

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_potec("data/PoTeC", readers=[0], texts=["b0"])
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, "0", "0_b0", canvas_size=(1680, 1050))

docs.title: load_onestop
docs.text:
load_onestop(
    root,
    *,
    regime="ordinary",
    parts=None,
    variant="public",
    download=False,
    names="source",
)

Load OneStop as normalized (words, fixations) frames, ready to plot.

OneStop's presentation monitor was 2560×1440 px (Dell U2715H; Berzak et al. 2025, Methods → Apparatus). Pass that as canvas_size to plot_scanpath for true-to-scale rendering. The reports already match the bundled demo's schema, so they load through the same auto-detection as any other data.

Parameters:

  • root (str | Path) –

    A folder holding the OneStop reports, or (public variant only) to download them into.

  • regime (str, default: 'ordinary' ) –

    "ordinary", "information_seeking", "repeated" or "information_seeking_repeated".

  • parts (Iterable[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Any subset of Title, Question_Preview, Paragraph, Questions, Answers, QA and Feedback. Left out, Paragraph.

  • variant (str, default: 'public' ) –

    "public" for the OSF release, "lacclab" for the lab's local export.

  • download (bool, default: False ) –

    Fetch the chosen regime and parts into root on first use. The public reports are large.

  • names (str, default: 'source' ) –

    "source" for OneStop's own column names, "canonical" for the internal ones (see api.load_scanpath_data).

Returns:

  • tuple[DataFrame, DataFrame] –

    The normalized (words, fixations) frames.

Examples:

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_onestop(
    "data/OneStop", regime="ordinary", parts=["Paragraph"], download=True
)
pid, tid = sps.list_trials(words, fixations).iloc[0]  # one reading
fig = sps.plot_scanpath(words, fixations, pid, tid, canvas_size=(2560, 1440))

docs.title: build_authored_scanpath
docs.text:
build_authored_scanpath(text, events=None, **layout_options)

Build normalized Words and Fixations frames from a hand-drawn scanpath.

Parameters:

  • text (str) –

    The text to lay out as word boxes. Explicit line breaks are kept.

  • events (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    The fixations, one row each, with the columns the app's Draw a scanpath table has (fixation_id, order_in_trial, word_id, x, y, duration_ms). Left out, each word gets one fixation at its center.

  • **layout_options (Any, default: {} ) –

docs.text:
plot_scanpath(
    words=None,
    fixations=None,
    participant=None,
    trial=None,
    *,
    screen=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    raw_gaze=None,
    drift_correction=None,
    drift_connectors=False,
    fix_index_range=None,
    illustration=False,
    illustration_label="auto",
    title="",
    caption="",
    column_names=None,
    **figure_overrides,
)

Build one trial's scanpath figure, by default in the app's Scanpath design.

Every figure option is a keyword (show_heatmap=True, color_by="pass_index", x_field="order_in_trial"), and figure_options lists them with their defaults. An option naming a column takes either name: frames under the dataset's own column names, as load_scanpath_data returns them by default, are read through the map they carry.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    A normalized words frame from load_scanpath_data, or None for a dataset recorded as raw gaze alone.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    The normalized fixations frame, or None likewise.

  • participant (str | None, default: None ) –

    The participant ID. It may be left out when the frames hold one trial.

  • trial (str | None, default: None ) –

    The trial ID. It may be left out when the frames hold one trial.

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    The screen of a multipart trial to draw. Left out, the first recorded screen; coordinate spaces are never concatenated.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    The monitor size in px, (width, height). Estimated from the data's extent by default; pass the real resolution ((2560, 1440) for OneStop) to keep coordinates true to scale.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    The base font size in px.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    The font family.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    Samples from load_raw_gaze, filtered to the trial and drawn as recorded, under the fixations. It can be the only table: with words and fixations None, the trial is looked up in the samples, the canvas is estimated from their extent, and the figure is the samples alone. No fixations are detected from them, so the fixation, saccade and heatmap layers stay empty.

  • drift_correction (str | None, default: None ) –

    Experimental. Without SCANPATH_EXPERIMENTAL=1, anything but None or "off" raises ValueError.

  • drift_connectors (bool, default: False ) –

    Experimental, with drift_correction.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    (start, end): draw only fixations start to end of the trial, 1-based and both inclusive. The app's Filters & highlights → Fixations → Index range.

  • illustration (bool, default: False ) –

    Apply the Illustration design: fixations snapped to their lines, arced saccades, one color for the fixations and one for the saccades, no heatmap or word boxes. Keywords you pass still win.

  • illustration_label (str, default: 'auto' ) –

    "auto" labels the figure an illustration when it no longer shows the data as recorded; "show" and "hide" decide it.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    A title band stamped onto the figure without shrinking the plot, like the app's Title & labels. Literal text, not the app's {trial_id}-style pattern, since you know which trial it is.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    A caption band, likewise.

  • column_names (dict | None, default: None ) –

    The column map for frames loaded with names="canonical" (data.column_names). The options then take the dataset's names too, and the figure's text uses them.

  • **figure_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    Any figure option, in place of the app's default. Three take a word of explanation:

    • palette= ("default", "print" or "high-contrast", or the app's names) sets a group of colors at once. A color you pass explicitly wins.
    • show_stimulus_image=True draws the trial's own stimulus page under the scanpath, as the app's Stimulus → Image does: the image_path its rows carry (from load_scanpath_data(image_root=…) or attach_stimulus_images; the bundled demo ships its pages), at its image_x / image_y. A background_image= you pass wins.
    • fixation_snap_to_line=True moves each fixation up or down onto its text line, keeping its x: its word's line, else the nearest. fixation_snap_position says where, in line heights from the line's middle (default −0.5, its top edge). The saccades' ends move with the markers, and it does nothing with show_fixations=False.

Returns:

  • Figure –

    The Plotly figure.

Raises:

  • TypeError –

    An unknown keyword. The message names the closest valid ones.

  • ValueError –

    A value an enumerated option does not take, or a color_by / highlight_column naming a column the trial's table doesn't have. The message names the closest ones.

Warns:

  • UserWarning –

    show_stimulus_image=True on a trial with no readable page (a PNG). The figure draws none.

docs.text:
animate_scanpath(
    words=None,
    fixations=None,
    participant=None,
    trial=None,
    *,
    screen=None,
    screen_b=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    playback_speed=1.0,
    autoplay=True,
    fix_index_range=None,
    fix_index_range_b=None,
    illustration_label="auto",
    title="",
    caption="",
    column_names=None,
    trial_b=None,
    dataset_b=None,
    setup=None,
    setup_b=None,
    **animation_overrides,
)

Build the animated replay of one trial's scanpath, or of two on one clock.

Save it as interactive HTML with save_figure, whose page keeps the replay's timing, or render it to GIF or MP4 with animation_export.export_animation, which keeps the same timing. fig.show() plays it on Plotly's frame queue, which runs slower than the reading did.

The replay takes a subset of plot_scanpath's options (figure_options("animation")), and the ones they share default alike, so the replay matches the static figure. The replay is made of fixations: it draws no raw gaze, and nothing detects fixations from samples.

Two scanpaths. trial_b co-animates a second trial, like the app's Animate + Compare. Both readings are drawn in A's coordinates, so a co-animation is an overlay, and a trial from another dataset has to share A's screen. Name that dataset with dataset_b (or give its setup_b), and the pair is checked the way compare_scanpaths checks an overlay. B's frames passed without either are taken to be from A's dataset, as render passes them for --compare-with alone, and are not checked: two readings of one corpus can span different extents, and inferring a canvas from each would refuse pairs that shared a screen.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • fixations (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • participant (str | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • trial (str | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    A's screen of a multipart trial, as in plot_scanpath.

  • screen_b (str | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen, looked up in B's own trial. Left out, its first recorded screen.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    A's monitor size, as in plot_scanpath.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    The base font size in px.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    The font family.

  • playback_speed (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    The replay lasts the reading time divided by this. Any other value than 1 makes the automatic Illustration label say the timing was changed.

  • autoplay (bool, default: True ) –

    Start the saved HTML's replay when it opens, at playback_speed. False saves it paused, to start with ▶ Play. A GIF or MP4 always plays from its first frame.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    (start, end): replay only that window of the trial's fixations, 1-based and inclusive. In a co-animation it windows A only, as in the app, where A's slider never cuts B.

  • fix_index_range_b (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    B's window, in a co-animation.

  • illustration_label (str, default: 'auto' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • column_names (dict | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • trial_b (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    B's (participant, trial). It is looked up in words_b / fixations_b when they are given, else in words / fixations, as compare_scanpaths takes it.

  • dataset_b (str | None, default: None ) –

    The name of B's dataset, when it is another one. The pair is then checked as an overlay, and B's participant IDs are prefixed with it, so a hover says which dataset the participant is from.

  • setup (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    A's experimental_setup.SetupSnapshot, the screen the overlay check reads. A side without one is read off its data: the extent of that one trial, which rarely spans the whole screen, so state both when you know them.

  • setup_b (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    B's.

  • **animation_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    Any figure option the replay takes. Also:

    • words_b / fixations_b: B's frames. Without trial_b they must hold one trial.
    • style_a / style_b: each scanpath's style, with the keys compare_scanpaths takes for markers and saccades (fix_color, marker_size_range, opacity, hollow, saccade_color, saccade_style, saccade_width), so the replay and the static comparison draw each trial alike. A lone replay ignores them.
    • fixation_flags_b: B's own fixation flags. None uses A's fixation_flags, or style_b's when it names some.
    • show_stimulus_image=True draws the trial's own page, as in plot_scanpath. A co-animation draws one page, under the text it draws: B's when compare_stimulus="b", else A's.
    • palette= works here too. Colors it implies that the replay doesn't take are dropped rather than raising, since you named a look, not those keys.

Returns:

  • Figure –

    The animated Plotly figure.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    The trial has no fixations (one recorded as raw gaze alone, or a words-only one). Also for raw_gaze=; draw samples with plot_scanpath(raw_gaze=…).

  • ValueError –

    An option the replay does not take (the message names the valid ones), a style naming saccade_classes (the replay has no saccade-class filter), or B frames holding several trials without trial_b.

  • IncomparableScreensError –

    B's dataset has a different canvas from A's. A ValueError.

compare_scanpaths(
    words,
    fixations,
    trial_a,
    trial_b,
    *,
    screen=None,
    screen_b=None,
    words_b=None,
    fixations_b=None,
    dataset_b="Dataset B",
    raw_gaze=None,
    raw_gaze_b=None,
    layout="overlay",
    compare_stimulus="both",
    setup=None,
    setup_b=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    labels=None,
    style_a=None,
    style_b=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    fix_index_range=None,
    fix_index_range_b=None,
    drift_correction=None,
    title="",
    caption="",
    column_names=None,
    **figure_overrides,
)

Build a figure comparing two scanpaths: the app's Compare mode.

Multipart trials. Each scanpath is one screen, never a whole multipart trial: every screen is its own coordinate space, so pooling them would draw saccades across page boundaries. list_parts() lists the screens.

Two datasets. words_b / fixations_b draw B from a different dataset. Two datasets can hold the same (participant_id, trial_id), so B's participant IDs are prefixed with dataset_b inside the merged frames. Without that, the figure could draw the wrong reading, or rows of both mixed into one. The frames you pass in are not modified, and only the trace labels show the prefix.

The overlay gate. An overlay needs both readings on screens of the same size, or it raises ValueError (the app falls back to side by side). That holds across datasets, and within one when the two screens carry different canvas_width / canvas_height or setup_b states another screen. Pass layout="side_by_side" or "stacked" to compare readings from different screens; each panel is then drawn to its own. Nothing is rescaled.

Per-scanpath style. style_a / style_b restyle one scanpath with these keys:

Key What it sets Left out fix_color, saccade_color The scanpath's colors Its default marker_size_range, opacity, hollow Its fixation markers Its default saccade_style, saccade_width Its saccade lines Its default box_color The outline of that reading's word boxes Its fix_color box_fill_color Their fill word_box_fill_color box_line_opacity, box_fill_opacity Their outline's and fill's opacity, 0–1 (0 hides it) word_box_line_opacity, word_box_fill_opacity raw_gaze_color That reading's raw-gaze samples Its fix_color heatmap_colorscale That reading's word-box heatmap color scale, on the range both share; two different scales get a color bar each heatmap_colorscale fixation_flags, saccade_classes That scanpath's own filters, in place of the figure's The figure's

The box keys and raw_gaze_color are this figure's only: the co-animation draws one set of boxes and no raw gaze, and ignores them.

Parameters:

  • words (DataFrame) –

    The words frame holding both trials, or A's when words_b is given.

  • fixations (DataFrame) –

    The fixations frame, likewise.

  • trial_a (tuple[str, str]) –

    A's (participant, trial).

  • trial_b (tuple[str, str]) –

    B's (participant, trial).

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    A's screen of a multipart trial. Left out, its first recorded screen, as in plot_scanpath.

  • screen_b (str | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen, looked up in B's own frames, so it may be a later page or another dataset's.

  • words_b (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    B's words frame, to draw B from another dataset.

  • fixations_b (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    B's fixations frame, likewise.

  • dataset_b (str, default: 'Dataset B' ) –

    The name B's participant IDs are prefixed with.

  • raw_gaze (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    Samples from load_raw_gaze, drawn under each reading's scanpath in its color. It serves both readings of one dataset; across datasets it is A's. Passing it turns the layer on; show_raw_gaze=False keeps it off.

  • raw_gaze_b (DataFrame | None, default: None ) –

    B's samples, across datasets.

  • layout (str, default: 'overlay' ) –

    "overlay", "side_by_side" ("side-by-side" also works) or "stacked".

  • compare_stimulus (str, default: 'both' ) –

    Whose word boxes and text an overlay draws: "both", "a" or "b". Two datasets' boxes coincide only when the text is identical. Split layouts ignore it, since each panel draws its own.

  • setup (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    A's experimental_setup.SetupSnapshot, the screen the overlay gate reads.

  • setup_b (SetupSnapshot | None, default: None ) –

    B's.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    A's monitor size, when you only have a resolution. Left out with setup, the canvas is read off the data.

  • labels (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    The two trace labels, when not the composed defaults.

  • style_a (dict | None, default: None ) –

    A's style, with the keys above.

  • style_b (dict | None, default: None ) –

    B's style.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    The base font size in px.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    The font family.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    (start, end): draw only that window of both scanpaths' fixations.

  • fix_index_range_b (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    B's own window, as the app's B slider sets it.

  • drift_correction (str | None, default: None ) –

    Experimental, as in plot_scanpath.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    As in plot_scanpath.

  • column_names (dict | None, default: None ) –

    As in plot_scanpath. A's names, or column_names, name the options and the figure's text; either dataset's frames may come under their own names.

  • **figure_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    Any figure option a comparison takes (figure_options("comparison")). Some act per scanpath:

    • fixation_flags and saccade_classes filter both scanpaths, unless a style gives one its own.
    • background_image is A's page. A split layout draws B's panel over background_image_b (with background_image_size_b / background_image_origin_b), and over nothing without it, never A's, since sharing a dataset says nothing about sharing a page.
    • show_stimulus_image=True takes each reading's own page from its rows: a split layout draws A's and B's, each in its panel, and an overlay the page of the text it draws (B's for compare_stimulus="b", else A's). An image passed explicitly wins.

Returns:

  • Figure –

    The Plotly figure.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    An overlay of two different screens (see the overlay gate), or a screen / screen_b the trial does not have or that names a screen of a single-screen trial.

  • TypeError –

    An unknown keyword. The message names the closest valid ones.

Set layers, colors, sizes and legends with keyword arguments to plot_scanpath, animate_scanpath or compare_scanpaths. The tables below list each option's default and matching CLI render flag, under the section names of the app's Plot controls. docs.title: Reproduce a figure in code
docs.text:
The app's Share tab → Code shows the Python or CLI code that rebuilds the figure on screen. Paste it into a notebook or a terminal to get the same figure. figure_code writes the same code without the app, and render --print-code prints it for a render command you already have.

print(
    sps.figure_code(
        participant="l7_1090",
        trial="l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele",
        show_heatmap=True,
        color_by="duration_ms",
    )
)

import scanpath_studio as sps

words, fixations = sps.load_sample_data()

fig = sps.plot_scanpath(
    words,
    fixations,
    participant='l7_1090',
    trial='l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele',
    canvas_size=(2560, 1440),
    color_by='duration_ms',
    show_heatmap=True,
)

sps.save_figure(fig, 'scanpath.png')

figure_code(
    *,
    kind="static",
    source="demo",
    source_options=None,
    participant="",
    trial="",
    screen=None,
    compare=None,
    compare_screen=None,
    compare_layout="overlay",
    compare_stimulus="both",
    compare_dataset="",
    compare_canvas=None,
    compare_labels=None,
    canvas_size=None,
    base_font_size=16,
    font_family=FONT_FAMILY,
    title="",
    caption="",
    fix_index_range=None,
    illustration_label="auto",
    drift_correction=None,
    drift_connectors=False,
    playback_speed=1.0,
    autoplay=True,
    flavor="python",
    explicit=False,
    output=None,
    **figure_overrides,
)

Write the API or CLI code that reproduces a figure.

The headless form of the app's Share → Code. Give it the arguments you would give plot_scanpath (kind="static"), animate_scanpath ("animation") or compare_scanpaths ("comparison"), and it returns the snippet that rebuilds that figure. Only the options that differ from figure_options are written, so the snippet stays readable. code_snippet.ReproductionCode is the structured form.

Parameters:

  • kind (str, default: 'static' ) –

    "static", "animation" or "comparison": the builder the snippet calls.

  • source (str, default: 'demo' ) –

    How the data is loaded: "demo", "synthetic", "files", "potec", "onestop", "author", "raw_gaze" (a dataset recorded as raw gaze alone, whose samples at source_options["raw_gaze"] are the data), or "unknown" for data a snippet can't name.

  • source_options (dict | None, default: None ) –

    That loader's arguments: {"root": …}, {"words": [...], "fixations": [...]} and so on. With show_raw_gaze=True, "raw_gaze" (and an optional "raw_gaze_schema") names the raw-gaze files; the demo uses its own.

  • participant (str, default: '' ) –

    The participant ID. Left empty, the snippet renders the first available trial, as render does.

  • trial (str, default: '' ) –

    The trial ID, likewise.

  • screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    A's screen of a multipart trial (screen=, --screen).

  • compare (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    B's (participant, trial), for a comparison or a co-animation.

  • compare_screen (str | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen (screen_b=, --compare-screen).

  • compare_layout (str, default: 'overlay' ) –

    The comparison's layout, as compare_scanpaths takes it.

  • compare_stimulus (str, default: 'both' ) –

    Whose stimulus an overlay draws, as compare_scanpaths takes it.

  • compare_dataset (str, default: '' ) –

    The dataset B was loaded from, when it is a second one. Both forms then load B's own tables, from the placeholder paths B_WORDS / B_FIXATIONS that you point at its files (words_b= / fixations_b= / dataset_b=, and --compare-words / --compare-fixations).

  • compare_canvas (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    B's screen, (width, height), with compare_dataset: written as setup_b= and --compare-canvas, which a co-animation across datasets needs.

  • compare_labels (tuple[str, str] | None, default: None ) –

    The two trace labels, when they are not the composed defaults: labels= and --label-a / --label-b.

  • canvas_size (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    The monitor size. Defaults to the screen render assumes for the source (the bundled demo's 2560×1440, PoTeC's 1680×1050, …), so both forms draw the same figure.

  • base_font_size (int, default: 16 ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • font_family (str, default: FONT_FAMILY ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • title (str, default: '' ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • caption (str, default: '' ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • fix_index_range (tuple[int, int] | None, default: None ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • illustration_label (str, default: 'auto' ) –

    As the builders take it.

  • drift_correction (str | None, default: None ) –

    Experimental, as in plot_scanpath.

  • drift_connectors (bool, default: False ) –

    Experimental, as in plot_scanpath.

  • playback_speed (float, default: 1.0 ) –

    As animate_scanpath takes it.

  • autoplay (bool, default: True ) –

    As animate_scanpath takes it.

  • flavor (str, default: 'python' ) –

    "python", "cli", or "both" (separated by a blank line).

  • explicit (bool, default: False ) –

    Write every option at its current value, not only the ones that differ from the defaults.

  • output (str | None, default: None ) –

    The file the snippet saves. Defaults to scanpath.html for an animation (render --animate writes only HTML) and to a PNG otherwise.

  • **figure_overrides (Any, default: {} ) –

    The figure options, as the builder takes them.

Returns:

  • str –

    The snippet. Anything neither form can reproduce (a raw-gaze table with no path to name, an uploaded stimulus image, B's rows from a second corpus) follows as # Note: comments, as the app's ⚠️ captions and the Note: lines render --print-code writes to stderr say it.

Raises:

  • ValueError –

    An unknown flavor.

  • TypeError –

    An option the builder does not take.

Examples:

print(
    sps.figure_code(
        participant="l7_1090",
        trial="l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele",
        show_heatmap=True,
        flavor="cli",
    )
)

save_figure(
    fig,
    path,
    *,
    scale=2,
    width=None,
    height=None,
    width_mm=None,
    width_in=None,
    dpi=None,
)

Save a figure, in the format its file extension names.

The file carries the citation of Scanpath Studio in its metadata — PNG text chunks, an SVG <metadata> element, the PDF's document properties, the HTML page's <head> — so a figure found later on its own still says how to cite it (cite prints it). Nothing is drawn.

Parameters:

  • fig (Figure) –

    The figure.

  • path (str | Path) –

    The file to write: .html (interactive), or .png, .svg or .pdf (static, through Kaleido; see the export FAQ for its setup).

  • scale (float, default: 2 ) –

    The static image's scale factor.

  • width (int | None, default: None ) –

    The image width in px, overriding the figure's own. Ignored for .html.

  • height (int | None, default: None ) –

    The image height in px, likewise.

  • width_mm (float | None, default: None ) –

    A PNG's print width in mm, as the app's Export → Current figure sets it: 180 mm at 600 dpi is a 4,252 px wide PNG, its height following the figure's aspect, with the dpi written into the file. It replaces scale.

  • width_in (float | None, default: None ) –

    The same in inches.

  • dpi (int | None, default: None ) –

    The resolution for width_mm / width_in. Default 300.

Returns:

  • Path –

    The path written.

Each visible layer (stimulus image, heatmap, word boxes, saccades, fixations, raw gaze, labels, frame) is the full figure with only that layer's elements, on a transparent background, at the same size and axis ranges. The files line up when stacked in Illustrator or Inkscape. The app's Export bundle writes the same files under Layers as separate files.

Parameters:

    A scanpath figure.

  • directory (str | Path) –

    The folder to write <layer>.<fmt> into.

  • fmt (str, default: 'svg' ) –

    Any save_figure extension without the dot. svg and pdf are vector and the best to edit; png and html work too.

  • scale (int, default: 2 ) –

    Passed to save_figure.

  • width (int | None, default: None ) –

    Passed to save_figure.

  • height (int | None, default: None ) –

    Passed to save_figure.

Returns:

  • dict –

    {layer: Path} for each file written.

docs.title: cache_status
docs.text:
cache_status()

Describe the recovery cache a local run keeps, without launching the app.

A local or desktop app stores completed uploaded datasets, column mappings, view settings, saved designs, metadata tables and annotations under your cache folder, so a refresh or a restart resumes where it left off. A hosted deployment, such as the online demo, keeps none. The same information is on the app's Data Management page under Saved on this computer, and in scanpath-studio cache.

Key What it holds enabled, directory Whether caching is on, and where exists, readable Whether its manifest is there and can be read datasets Each stored dataset's name, per-frame row counts and size in bytes rows, bytes, saved_at The totals, and when it was last written annotations, designs, metadata, settings What else is stored damaged Each stored dataset whose entry or files are broken, with the reason. The app restores the others and keeps that one rather than dropping it damaged_metadata Why the stored metadata tables would not restore; "" when they would

Returns:

    The status, as a dict with the keys above. Delete the cache with clear_cache.

docs.title: clear_cache
docs.text:
clear_cache()

Delete the recovery cache.

Removes only the files the app wrote (manifest.json and the datasets' Parquet files); anything else in the folder is left alone. A running local app writes its session back out at its next change, so start it with scanpath-studio run --no-persist or SCANPATH_STUDIO_PERSIST=0 to stop that.

Returns:

  • dict –

    The cache's status afterwards, as cache_status gives it.

docs.text:
cite(format='bibtex', corpus=None)

How to cite Scanpath Studio — and, optionally, the corpus you used.

The same entries as the app's Help → About and Cite buttons, and scanpath-studio cite. Every figure, replay and page save_figure writes also carries the citation in its file metadata.

print(sps.cite())                       # BibTeX

    "onestop" or "potec" to add that corpus's citation after the software's; None for the software alone.

Returns:

    The citation as text (APA without Markdown).

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
scanpath-studio launches the app. Its subcommands do the rest without opening it:

Command What it does scanpath-studio, run Launch the app render Write one trial's scanpath, heatmap or replay to a file corpus Render a corpus figure from a tidy CSV you already have check Run the Data checks on your tables cache Show or clear the recovery cache version Show the build, and whether a newer release is out cite Print how to cite Scanpath Studio

Each command takes --help, and scanpath-studio --version prints the version. A word that is not a command is an error that suggests the closest command. It is not passed on to Streamlit.

docs.title: Launch the app
docs.text:
scanpath-studio
scanpath-studio --server.port 8600
scanpath-studio --no-persist          # don't cache the session on this computer
scanpath-studio --download-dir D:\corpora  # where ⬇ Download saves public datasets

scanpath-studio run … is the same. Any other launch flag is passed on to streamlit run.

The app listens on this computer only (127.0.0.1), and it has no login. To serve it to other machines on a network you trust, pass --server.address 0.0.0.0, or set server.address in a Streamlit config.toml or STREAMLIT_SERVER_ADDRESS:

scanpath-studio --server.address 0.0.0.0

Served on a network, the app turns off the controls that read or write the server's folders, because any visitor could use them. These are the Data directory box, the folder picker, and ⬇ Download for the public datasets and stimulus-image folders. On a lab server you trust, turn them back on with SCANPATH_LOCAL_FS=1 (SCANPATH_LOCAL_FS=1 scanpath-studio --server.address 0.0.0.0).

docs.title: render
docs.text:
render writes one trial to a file without opening the app. The extension picks the format: .html is interactive and needs nothing else, while .png, .svg and .pdf need Chrome, Chromium or Edge (or run plotly_get_chrome -y once; see the FAQ). The figure is the app's Scanpath design unless a flag changes it, and every figure option has a flag.

# List the trials to pick from
scanpath-studio render --sample --list-trials

# The bundled demo
scanpath-studio render --sample -o scanpath.html

# Your own data (replace p1 / t3 with IDs from --list-trials)
scanpath-studio render \
  --words ia.csv --fixations fixations.csv \
  --participant p1 --trial t3 --output scanpath.svg

# A draft file saved from the app's Draw a scanpath screen
scanpath-studio render --authoring authored-scanpath.json -o authored.html

# A public dataset, loaded as the app loads it (downloaded on first use)
scanpath-studio render --potec ./potec --list-trials
scanpath-studio render --onestop ./onestop --onestop-variant public \
  --onestop-regime ordinary --onestop-part Paragraph --list-trials

The Python API loads the same datasets with load_potec and load_onestop.

docs.title: Common tasks
docs.text: Goal Flags add a layer --word-boxes, --fixation-index, --heatmap hide a layer --no-text, --no-fixations, --no-saccades animate --animate, optionally --playback-speed X. The replay uses every styling flag it can draw and names the rest in a warning set the screen size --canvas WIDTHxHEIGHT. --crop-to-data frames the data instead of the whole screen, with --crop-margin PX around it (default: 5% of the data's extent, at least 20 px) color fixations --color-by FIELD, including a column of your own once --keep-columns COLUMN… carries it through loading size fixations by duration --marker-size-scale sqrt\|linear\|log\|relative (default sqrt), --marker-duration-range LO HI (ms, default 50 600), --marker-size-range MIN MAX (px), --no-duration-size-legend draw only part of a trial --fix-index-range START:END (1-based, both inclusive; --animate and --compare-with honor it too) draw the stimulus --stimulus-image PATH for one image. --show-stimulus-image draws each trial's stimulus image, named in the image_path column (--sample ships its images). --image-root DIR --image-pattern '{text_id}.png' fills image_path from a folder smooth the heatmap --heatmap-style smoothed --heatmap-sigma 20 (σ in px; leave it out for an automatic σ) style the word boxes --word-box-color, --word-box-line-opacity, --word-box-fill-color, --word-box-fill-opacity. A fill opacity of 0 draws outlines only, and a line opacity of 0 the fill only size the figure --width, --height, --scale. For print, --width-mm MM or --width-in IN with --dpi N (default 300) add a title and caption --title, --caption write each layer to its own file --separable-layers print the equivalent code --print-code python (or cli / both), plus --print-code-explicit

docs.title: Compare two scanpaths
docs.text:
--compare-with PARTICIPANT:TRIAL draws a second trial, B, beside or over the first. It does what the app's Compare does.

# Two participants on the same paragraph, overlaid
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele -o compare.html

# The same overlay, drawing only B's word boxes and text
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele --compare-stimulus b \
  -o compare_b.html

# Side by side: each panel draws its trial's stimulus
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele \
  --compare-layout side-by-side -o compare.svg

# A style for each scanpath
scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_1_1_Ele \
  --compare-with l7_1090:l7_1090_2_1_1_Ele \
  --style-a fix_color=#D55E00,opacity=0.5 --style-b saccade_style=dash \
  -o compare_styled.html

# B from a second dataset
scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv -p p1 -t t1 \
  --compare-with p1:t1 \
  --compare-words other/ia.csv --compare-fixations other/fix.csv \
  --compare-dataset-name "Our lab" \
  --canvas 1680x1050 --compare-canvas 1680x1050 \
  -o cross.html
Goal Flags pick B --compare-with PARTICIPANT:TRIAL pick each screen of a multipart trial --screen ID (A), --compare-screen ID (B); each defaults to its trial's first screen arrange the panels --compare-layout {overlay,side-by-side,stacked} (default overlay) choose whose stimulus an overlay draws --compare-stimulus {both,a,b} (default both) name the two scanpaths --label-a TEXT --label-b TEXT (both or neither) style each scanpath --style-a SPEC, --style-b SPEC (keys below) leave out the A/B legend --no-compare-legend give B a separate stimulus image (side by side or stacked) --stimulus-image-b PATH, with --stimulus-image-size-b WxH / --stimulus-image-origin-b X,Y take B from another dataset --compare-words PATH… --compare-fixations PATH…, plus --compare-raw-gaze PATH… and --compare-dataset-name NAME set the two screen sizes --canvas WxH, --compare-canvas WxH replay both on one clock add --animate (HTML output)

--label-a / --label-b and --style-a / --style-b apply to the --animate replay too.

docs.title: Style keys
docs.text:
--style-a and --style-b take a comma-separated KEY=VALUE list and can be repeated. They are the app's Scanpath A / Scanpath B rows and compare_scanpaths's style_a / style_b. A key left out keeps that scanpath's default.

Key Value Left out fix_color #RRGGBB that scanpath's default saccade_color #RRGGBB that scanpath's default box_color #RRGGBB, the outline of that scanpath's word boxes its fix_color box_fill_color #RRGGBB, the boxes' fill --word-box-fill-color box_line_opacity, box_fill_opacity 0–1 --word-box-line-opacity, --word-box-fill-opacity raw_gaze_color #RRGGBB, that scanpath's raw-gaze samples its fix_color heatmap_colorscale a Plotly color scale; the range stays shared, and two different scales get a color bar each --heatmap-colorscale saccade_style solid, dash, dot or dashdot that scanpath's default saccade_width px that scanpath's default marker_size_range MIN:MAX that scanpath's default opacity 0.1–1 that scanpath's default hollow true or false that scanpath's default

The --animate replay draws one set of word boxes and no raw gaze, so it ignores the box_* keys and raw_gaze_color.

docs.title: What a comparison can't combine
docs.text:
• --compare-with cannot be combined with --all-screens or --screens. A comparison is one figure of two trials, each drawn from one screen. B's --compare-screen is looked up in B's trial, so it can be a later screen, or a screen of the second dataset.
  • An overlay of two datasets needs matching canvases. On two different canvases, --compare-layout overlay exits with an error, and so does --animate, which replays both scanpaths in one coordinate space. Use --compare-layout side-by-side or stacked, without --animate. Two screens of one dataset with different canvases are refused the same way. Nothing is rescaled.
  • Without --compare-canvas, the second dataset's screen size is estimated from its data, as A's is when neither --canvas nor a built-in source gives one. The data rarely spans the whole screen, so give both screen sizes when you know them.
  • A second dataset can only be loaded from files. In Python, compare_scanpaths takes B's frames directly, so any dataset you can load can be B.

docs.title: Raw gaze
docs.text:
--raw-gaze PATH… reads a Raw gaze table, with its columns auto-detected like --fixations, and draws the plotted trial's samples under the fixations. With --compare-with it covers both scanpaths, each in its scanpath's color. --compare-raw-gaze PATH… gives B's samples when B comes from another dataset. --animate ignores raw gaze with a warning.

scanpath-studio render --sample -p l37_1129 -t l37_1129_2_2_2_Adv \
  --sample-raw-gaze --raw-gaze-opacity 0.4 -o raw_gaze.html

When --raw-gaze is the only input, it is the dataset. --list-trials lists its trials, and render draws the chosen trial's samples as recorded. No fixations are detected from them, so --animate and --compare-with exit with an error that says so.

scanpath-studio render --raw-gaze gaze_samples.csv --list-trials
scanpath-studio render --raw-gaze gaze_samples.csv -t t3 -o samples.png

docs.title: Multipart trials and many trials
docs.text:
render writes one trial per run. For many figures, use the Python batch recipe or the Export bundle on the app's Export tab.

A multipart trial is the exception. --all-screens writes one __screen-001-<id> file per screen of the selected trial, and --screens Title,Paragraph writes only the screens named, each still numbered by its place in the trial. When your tables have no screen column, --trial-parts-manifest manifest.json assigns source rows to screens.

scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv --list-parts
scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv \
  -p p1 -t t3 --screen question -o question.svg
scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv \
  -p p1 -t t3 --all-screens --animate --screen-transition recorded \
  -o replay.html

docs.title: When a column isn't recognized
docs.text:
Column names are auto-detected (EyeLink, Tobii, SMI, Pupil Labs, Gazepoint and snake_case spellings). When one isn't, render stops and prints which field it could not find, the names it looked for, the columns your table has, and a mapping to start from. Pass that mapping back as JSON, inline or as a path to a .json file, with --word-schema (the --words table) and/or --fix-schema (the --fixations table). check takes the same two flags.

scanpath-studio render --words ia.csv --fixations fix.csv \
  --word-schema '{"trial": "TRIAL_LABEL", "word_id": "IA_ID", "text": "IA_LABEL",
                  "left": "IA_LEFT", "right": "IA_RIGHT", "top": "IA_TOP", "bottom": "IA_BOTTOM"}' \
  --fix-schema fix_schema.json -o scanpath.html

A mapping replaces auto-detection for that table, so it has to name every required field, not only the one that failed. It is the same dict load_scanpath_data(word_schema=…, fix_schema=…) takes in Python.

docs.title: render flags
docs.text: Every render flag, generated from the command's parser, with the defaults and help that --help prints. The figure flags are grouped like the figure options they set.

docs.title: Trial and output
docs.text: Option Value Default Description -p--participant PARTICIPANT — Participant ID (default: the first). -t--trial TRIAL — Trial ID (default: the participant's first). --screen SCREEN — Screen ID within a multipart trial (default: the first screen). --list-trials switch — Print every trial with its participant, trial and text IDs, then exit. Pass a trial ID to -t. --list-parts switch — Print the screens of each multipart trial in order, then exit. -p and -t narrow the list. --all-screens switch — Render every screen of the selected trial, one file each. The screen ID goes before the output's extension. --screens ID[,ID...] — Like --all-screens, for only these screens: comma-separated screen IDs, e.g. Title,Paragraph. See --list-parts. --screen-transition instant, recorded instant With --all-screens --animate: record no delay between screens (instant) or the recorded one (recorded) in each file's metadata (default: instant). -o--output PATH — Output file. Its extension sets the format: .html, .png, .svg or .pdf. --animate switch — Render the animated replay instead of the static figure (HTML only).

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --sample switch — Use the bundled demo, from OneStop: 2 participants, 12 trials each (--list-trials shows them). --authoring PATH — A draft file from the app's Draw a scanpath screen. --words PATH [PATH ...] — The Words table: CSV, TSV, TXT, TAB, Parquet, Feather, XLSX or XLS, or a .zip of them. Columns are auto-detected from EyeLink, Gazepoint, Tobii, SMI, Pupil Labs and snake_case names. Several paths, or a quoted glob, are stacked into one table. --fixations PATH [PATH ...] — The Fixations table, in the formats --words reads and auto-detected the same way. Several paths, or a quoted glob, are stacked into one table (e.g. one file per participant). --image-root DIR — A folder of stimulus images. Each row's image is found with --image-pattern and stored in its image_path column. Add --show-stimulus-image to draw them. Works with every input, including --sample and the public datasets. --image-pattern PATTERN {text_id}.png File name pattern inside --image-root, with column placeholders, e.g. '{text_id}.png' or '{participant_id}/{trial_id}.png'. --trial-parts-manifest PATH — A JSON manifest that assigns source rows to the screens of each trial, in order. Use it with --words / --fixations when the tables have no screen column. --word-schema JSON — Column mapping for the --words table, replacing auto-detection. A JSON object from each field to a column name, or the path of a JSON file holding one, e.g. '{"trial": "TRIAL_INDEX", "word_id": "IA_ID", ...}'. It is the dict api.load_scanpath_data takes. Needed only when a column isn't recognized, and the error then prints a mapping to start from. --fix-schema JSON — Column mapping for the --fixations table, replacing auto-detection. A JSON object from each field to a column name, or the path of a JSON file holding one, e.g. '{"trial": "TRIAL_INDEX", "word_id": "IA_ID", ...}'. It is the dict api.load_scanpath_data takes. Needed only when a column isn't recognized, and the error then prints a mapping to start from. --keep-columns COLUMN [COLUMN ...] — More columns to keep through loading, under the names they have in your files (e.g. a pupil size), from whichever table has them. Without it, loading keeps only the mapped and recognized fields. A kept fixation column can be used by --color-by, an axis or a hover. Same as keep_columns= in api.load_scanpath_data. --potec DIR — Load the PoTeC corpus (DiLi-Lab/PoTeC) from DIR, downloading the files it needs (~45 MB) on first use. It has 75 participants, with IDs between 0 and 105 (--list-trials shows them). A trial is one participant reading one text, named <participant>_<text> (e.g. 0_b0). The texts are b0–b5 and p0–p5. --onestop DIR — Load the OneStop corpus from DIR. The public variant downloads the reports for the chosen regime and parts from OSF on first use, tens to hundreds of MB each. The lacclab variant reads a local export. Choose with --onestop-regime, --onestop-part and --onestop-variant. --onestop-regime ordinary, information_seeking, repeated, information_seeking_repeated ordinary OneStop reading regime for --onestop (default: ordinary). --onestop-part Title, Question_Preview, Paragraph, Questions, Answers, QA, Feedback — OneStop trial part for --onestop. Repeatable (default: Paragraph). With several, each part is a separate trial. --onestop-variant public, lacclab public OneStop source for --onestop: public, downloaded from OSF, or lacclab, a local lab-processed export with no download. --participant-metadata FILE [FILE ...] — A participant metadata table: one row per participant, with a participant ID column and any other fields. Several files, or a glob, are stacked into one table. Its rows are checked against the loaded participants and reported, and its fields are added to the --list-trials output. --trial-metadata FILE [FILE ...] — A trial metadata table: one row per trial, with a trial ID column and any other fields. Several files, or a glob, are stacked into one table. It is checked and reported the same way, and its fields are added to the --list-trials output. --trial-metadata-participant-column--trial-metadata-reader-column COLUMN — Key the --trial-metadata table by participant and trial, with this column as the participant ID. Without it, the table is keyed by trial ID alone, and each row applies to every participant's reading of that trial. This is never guessed from the file. --text-metadata FILE [FILE ...] — A text metadata table: one row per text, with a text ID column and any other fields. Several files, or a glob, are stacked into one table. It is checked and reported the same way, and its fields are added to the --list-trials output. It is keyed by text alone, never by participant.

docs.title: Fixations
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --no-fixations switch — Hide the fixations. --fixation-index switch — Number the fixations in order (the app's Fixation index). --no-fixation-index--no-order switch — Hide the fixation numbers (the default). --snap-fixations switch — Move each fixation up or down onto its text line: its word's line, else the nearest. Its x stays. --snap-position sets where on the line. --snap-position LINES — Where on its line a snapped fixation sits, in line heights from the line's middle: 0 centers it, -0.5 is the top edge, 0.5 the bottom edge (default: -0.5). Used with --snap-fixations. --palette {default,print,high-contrast} — Color palette (the app's Palette): default (colorblind-safe, Okabe–Ito), print (grayscale, for black-and-white printing) or high-contrast. The app's palette names work too. Each --*-color flag overrides it. --color-by FIELD — Fixations table column to color the fixations by, e.g. duration_ms, or 'line' for each fixation's text line (same as --color-by-line). Default: '(uniform)', one color, since marker size already shows duration. --fixation-color COLOR — Fixation color when --color-by is '(uniform)' (default: #0072B2). --fixation-symbol circle, square, diamond, triangle-up, cross, x, star, hexagon, heart — Fixation marker shape. Unlike color, shape survives a grayscale print (default: circle). --fixation-colorscale NAME — Color scale for --color-by, e.g. Viridis (default: Blues). --marker-size-range MIN MAX — Smallest and largest fixation marker size in px, e.g. 4 12 (default: 8 24). A smaller range suits thumbnails. --marker-size-scale sqrt, linear, log, relative — How duration sets marker size (default: sqrt). sqrt, linear and log map --marker-duration-range onto --marker-size-range, so a duration gets the same size in every trial, comparison and replay. With sqrt, marker area grows with duration. relative stretches each figure from its shortest to its longest fixation. --marker-duration-range LO HI — The durations in ms that get the smallest and largest marker (default: 50 600). Shorter and longer fixations are clamped to them. Not used by --marker-size-scale relative. --fixation-opacity O — Fixation marker opacity, 0.1–1.0 (default: 0.7, so overlapping fixations show through). --fixation-outline-width PX — Outline width around each filled fixation marker, 0–5 px; 0 draws none (default: 0.5). --fixation-outline-color COLOR — Color of that outline (default: #111111). --hollow-fixations switch — Draw the fixations as outlines instead of filled markers. --color-by-line switch — Color each fixation by the text line it lands on, with the lines found from the word boxes. Overrides --color-by. Same as --color-by line. --fixation-color-range LO HI — Fix the --color-by color scale to LO..HI instead of the trial's range, so several figures share one scale. --order-font-size PX — Size of the fixation index numbers (default: 10). --order-font-color COLOR — Color of the fixation index numbers (default: #111111). --no-fixation-colorbar switch — Leave out --color-by's color bar. --fixation-colorbar-orientation vertical, horizontal — Fixation color bar: beside the plot (vertical, default) or below it. --fixation-colorbar-tickangle DEG — Fixation color bar: tick-label angle, -90–90 (default: 0). --fixation-colorbar-tickfont-size PX — Fixation color bar: tick-label size (default: 12). --fixation-colorbar-thickness PX — Fixation color bar: thickness, 4–40 px (default: 14). --fixation-colorbar-length F — Fixation color bar: length as a share of the plot's side, 0.1–1.0 (default: a third of its height upright, 0.6 of its width lying down).

docs.title: Saccades
docs.text: Option Value Default Description --no-saccades switch — Hide the saccades. --saccade-arrows switch — Draw an arrowhead on each saccade (the app's Direction arrows). --saccade-color COLOR — Saccade line and arrow color, as hex or a CSS name (default: #CC79A7). --saccade-style solid, dash, dot, dashdot — Saccade line dash style (default: solid). --saccade-width PX — Saccade line width in px, 0.5–10 (default: 2). --saccade-opacity O — Opacity of the saccade lines and arrows, 0.1–1.0 (default: 1). In a comparison, both scanpaths share it. --saccade-arrow-size PX — Size of the --saccade-arrows arrowheads, 4–40 px (default: 12). --saccade-color-by-type switch — Color each saccade by its type: forward, skip, refixation, return sweep or regression (the app's By type). --saccade-color-by-direction switch — Color each saccade as forward or regression (the app's Forward / regression). --saccade-type-color CLASS=COLOR — Set one saccade type's color, e.g. --saccade-type-color regression=#000000. Repeatable. Types: forward, skip, refixation, return_sweep, regression. Implies --saccade-color-by-type. With --saccade-color-by-direction, it sets the forward and regression colors instead. --saccade-arcs switch — Draw saccades as upward arcs instead of straight lines (the app's Shape: Arc).
